title: Exploring the Link Between Artificial Sweetener Consumption and COPD: Insights From NHANES Data, Machine Learning, Multi-Omics, and Experimental Validation.
abstract: Artificial sweeteners (AS) are an emerging environmental pollutant. Few studies have focused on the link between AS consumption and the risk of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). This study integrates NHANES, GEO, and sceQTL data, utilizing methods such as longitudinal studies, toxicity analysis, machine learning, MR analysis, molecular docking, and in vitro experiments to investigate the relationship between AS consumption and COPD risk, as well as the underlying molecular mechanisms. NHANES data analysis showed an association between AS consumption and increased COPD risk. Toxicity predictions indicated that AS exhibits respiratory toxicity, with several AS compounds posing acute toxicity risks to susceptible populations under specific conditions. Bioinformatics analyses of COPD datasets identified key modules and genes, which, together with AS-related targets from chemical databases, revealed 10 candidate genes. Machine learning further pinpointed 8 key genes (CDKN1A, F13A1, IL6, PLA2G2A, PTGS2, S100A8, SERPINE1, and THBS1), all significantly upregulated in COPD and enriched in pathways related to inflammation, immune response, and apoptosis. MR analysis confirmed that a causal link exists between the expression of CDKN1A, F13A1, IL6, and S100A8 in specific immune cells and COPD risk. title: Macrophage membrane-coated nanoparticles control pathological inflammation and enhance survival in models of severe bacterial pneumonia.
abstract: Rationale Severe bacterial pneumonia is a leading cause of death worldwide, and mortality rates remain unacceptably high despite appropriate antibiotic treatment. Macrophage membrane-coated nanoparticles (MΦ-NPs) are biomimetic constructs engineered to neutralize bacterial toxins, pathogen-associated molecular patterns, and proinflammatory cytokines. Objective To evaluate the therapeutic potential of MΦ-NPs for the treatment of severe bacterial pneumonia. Methods We evaluated the therapeutic potential of MΦ-NPs using in vitro models of infection involving human lung endothelial and epithelial cells, as well as primary human neutrophils, and in vivo murine models of Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) pneumonia. Main results MΦ-NPs demonstrated potent cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory activity in vitro, without impairing neutrophil antimicrobial function. In both PA and MRSA pneumonia models, MΦ-NP treatment significantly improved survival, reduced bacterial burden, lowered proinflammatory cytokines, and preserved lung architecture. Quantitative proteomics further revealed suppression of inflammatory, coagulation, and fibrotic pathways associated with poor outcomes in human pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome. Conclusions These findings establish MΦ-NPs as a promising host-directed therapeutic strategy for mitigating the deleterious inflammatory sequelae of severe bacterial pneumonia.

title: <b><b>Safety profile and potential favorable reporting signals of liraglutide in patients with ulcerative colitis: A FAERS pharmacovigilance and network pharmacology study</b></b>.
abstract: Background Liraglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA), has preclinical anti-inflammatory and barrier-protective effects, but its safety profile and potential favorable reporting associations in ulcerative colitis (UC) remain uncertain. Objectives To characterize liraglutide-associated reports in patients with UC and explore biological pathways that may contextualize the observed pharmacovigilance signals. Methods Reports submitted to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) from January 1, 2013, to December 31, 2025, were analyzed in which liraglutide was recorded as the primary suspected drug and UC as the indication. Disproportionality was assessed using the reporting odds ratio (ROR), proportional reporting ratio (PRR), Bayesian confidence propagation neural network (BCPNN) and multi-item gamma Poisson shrinker (MGPS). Network pharmacology identified shared targets, constructed a protein-protein interaction network and performed Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment analyses. Results Among 5,903 unique cases and 28,607 preferred-term event entries, the most frequent categories were general disorders and administration-site conditions, gastrointestinal disorders, injury or medication-related complications, infections and investigations. title: 2026 Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) strategy report: executive summary and key changes. From population evidence to personalized asthma care.
abstract: The Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) strategy report provides a comprehensive, annually updated evidence-based approach to asthma diagnosis, assessment, treatment, and prevention across the lifespan. Its central approach is personalized, iterative care based on the Assess-Adjust-Review cycle for both symptom control and reduction of future risk (including severe exacerbations, persistent airflow limitation, and treatment-related harm). GINA emphasizes objective confirmation of diagnosis wherever possible, and regular assessment of lung function, inhaler technique, adherence, multimorbidity, risk factors (including type 2 biomarkers), and patient goals and preferences. GINA strongly recommends that all adults, adolescents, children, and most preschoolers with asthma should receive inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)-containing treatment. GINA recommends against short-acting β2-agonist (SABA)-only treatment. For adults/adolescents, GINA Track 1, using low-dose ICS-formoterol, an anti-inflammatory reliever (AIR), either as-needed-only or as maintenance-and-reliever therapy, is preferred because of its substantial reduction in severe exacerbations compared with SABA-based regimens, and its simplicity. Age-specific treatment pathways in children also emphasize ICS-containing therapy and exacerbation prevention. title: Incretins predict response to enteral nutrition strategies in the Early versus Delayed Enteral Nutrition trial: a secondary analysis.
abstract: Rationale The Early versus Delayed Enteral Nutrition (EDEN) trial found no significant difference in mortality between trophic and full enteral nutrition strategies in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) patients. Heterogeneity of treatment effect (HTE) has been identified in prior ARDS trials. We previously identified intestine-derived incretin hormones (glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide [GIP] and glucagon-like peptide [GLP]-1) as potential predictive biomarkers in the response to nutrition. Objectives To investigate incretins as biomarkers predictive of HTE in EDEN. Methods Glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide, GLP-1, and host immune response biomarkers were measured from pre-intervention EDEN plasma samples. We investigated HTE with 60-day mortality as a primary outcome by testing interaction of treatment with circulating incretin levels in analyses adjusted for demographics, severity of illness, diabetes mellitus, and circulating IL-6 and assessed mortality by treatment arm across incretin tertiles. We additionally tested for HTE by de novo ARDS subphenotypes and by risk of mortality. Measurements and main results A total of 889 participants were included (452 randomly assigned to trophic and 437 to full enteral nutrition). This inconsistency probably reflects the inherently dynamic nature of wound healing and the complexity of targeting cellular senescence. title: Age-dependent remodeling of the peripheral nerve microenvironment: anatomical implications for perineural invasion
abstract: Perineural invasion (PNI) involves interactions between malignant cells and the cellular and extracellular components of peripheral nerves. Although substantial evidence implicates Schwann cells, immune cells, and neurotrophic signaling in this process, the biological age of the invaded nerve has received limited attention. Peripheral nerves undergo age-related changes in Schwann-cell plasticity, inflammatory responses, and regenerative capacity, potentially altering the microenvironment encountered by invading tumor cells. We propose that peripheral nerve aging may influence PNI through changes in glial behavior, extracellular matrix organization, and the functional integrity of neural compartments. These mechanisms could have opposing effects: persistent inflammatory and senescence-associated signals might facilitate invasion, whereas reduced Schwann-cell plasticity might limit tumor-supportive repair programs. Current evidence does not establish which effect predominates. We outline an anatomically informed framework for investigating this hypothesis through age-comparative nerve models, compartment-specific histopathology, and spatial molecular profiling. Particular attention is given to the endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium as distinct anatomical environments that may differentially influence tumor–nerve interactions. title: Lipid droplet dysmetabolism affects cell homeostasis in an in vitro model of Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Lipid droplets (LD) are dynamic organelles involved in neutral lipid storage, energy homeostasis, and protection against lipotoxicity and oxidative stress. Dysregulated LD metabolism has emerged as a pathological hallmark of several neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease (AD). In this study, we investigated alterations in LD metabolism and their impact on mitochondria-associated membranes (MAM) using an in vitro AD model, namely mouse neuroblastoma N2A cells overexpressing the amyloid precursor protein carrying the familial Swedish mutation (APPswe). APPswe cells exhibited a marked depletion of LD accompanied by the accumulation of free fatty acids and triacylglycerol (TAG). These cells also displayed reduced levels of seipin, a key regulator of LD biogenesis and maintenance, potentially contributing to impaired TAG storage and LD formation. These lipid alterations were associated with increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and lipid peroxidation, suggesting impaired stress buffering capacity. Pharmacological modulation of diacylglycerol acyltransferase 1 (DGAT1), a key enzyme in TAG synthesis, was associated with an increase in LD size, improved endoplasmic reticulum-mitochondria contacts, and enhanced mitochondrial function in APPswe cells. title: Latest Concepts in Meniscal Allograft Transplantation.
abstract: Meniscal allograft transplantation has evolved to a standard-of-care procedure for selected symptomatic patients with meniscal deficiency. Clinical success is highly dependent on rigorous patient selection and optimization of the joint environment, often necessitating concomitant procedures such as anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction or corrective osteotomies to ensure graft longevity. Although bony fixation techniques have traditionally been considered the biomechanical gold standard, soft-tissue fixation techniques demonstrate comparable clinical outcomes. Long-term data suggest that meniscal allograft transplantation is a durable intervention, with 10-year survivorship rates ranging from 73.5% to 85%. Recent progress in areas such as synthetic grafts, artificial intelligence for preoperative planning, and three-dimensional bioprinted scaffolds could further improve outcomes and potentially decrease or even eliminate the dependence on cadaver grafts. However, much further development is required before these technologies are fully realized.

title: Social comparison via physical activity leaderboards: perceptions, preferences, and implications for physical activity promotion among insufficiently active adults.
abstract: Social comparison is often used to promote physical activity (PA; e.g., via leaderboards that rank users' PA behavior), but their utility among insufficiently active adults is unclear. Our aim was to describe these adults' perceptions of social comparison, broadly and in the context of PA leaderboards. Participants (N = 21; M Age = 36 years; M BMI = 30.5 kg/m 2 ; 33% men; 62% from underrepresented groups in the United States) completed a survey and a semi-structured interview; they described their perceptions of social comparison and leaderboards and their reactions to images of a PA leaderboard interface. We used reflexive thematic analysis with member checking to generate and refine five themes: (1) a shift in overall attitudes toward comparison (from negative to neutral/mixed); (2) responses depend on person-level traits and situational factors; (3) even without context, leaderboards prompt emotional responses; (4) openness to PA leaderboards for motivating PA; and (5) desire for ways to connect with others around PA. Although comparison was initially perceived as negative, leaderboards were described positively. We present potential explanations for this discrepancy-including perceptions of distinct purposes for leaderboards versus comparison more broadly-as well as considerations for future work. Overall, findings suggest the potential acceptability of leaderboards to support PA promotion among insufficiently active adults, and their effects on PA motivation and behavior

title: Millennial-Scale Persistence and Long-Term Dormancy of Bloom-Forming Cyanobacteria in the Baltic Sea Revealed by Viable Resting Stages and Sedimentary Ancient DNA.
abstract: Blooms of filamentous diazotrophic cyanobacteria (Nostocales) have occurred in the Baltic Sea for millennia but are expected to intensify under ongoing climate warming and eutrophication, with consequences for ecosystem health. Nostocales form resting stages (akinetes) that are preserved in sediments, enabling reconstruction of past bloom dynamics. We investigated past and contemporary variability in the abundance of bloom-forming Nostocales by analysing akinetes and sedimentary ancient DNA (sedaDNA) metabarcoding from central Baltic Sea sediments, spanning ~7200 calibrated years before present (cal yr BP). Akinete viability was assessed by dead-cell staining and fluorescence microscopy. Akinetes were present back to ~3580 cal yr BP, with 98% remaining viable for up to 200 years and the oldest viable akinete persisting up to ~1450 years, highlighting resilience in hypoxic Baltic Sea sediments. SedaDNA extended the Nostocales record back to ~7150 cal yr BP. Both parameters showed a significant increase in Nostocales abundance since the 1990s, likely driven by past anthropogenic nutrient inputs before and ongoing climate warming in the Baltic Sea. The findings highlight the value of a multi-parameter approach, while discrepancies between akinete and sedaDNA records underscore the complexity of reconstructing past cyanobacterial abundance from sedimentary archives.
summary_short: SedaDNA extended the Nostocales record back to ~7150 cal yr BP.

title: Prevalence and Associated Factors of Sarcopenia in Middle-Aged and Older Adults in Korea: Applying the AWGS 2025.
abstract: Background This study examined sarcopenia prevalence and explored associated factors among community-dwelling middle-aged and older adults in Korea using the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia (AWGS) 2025 criteria. Methods We analysed 5600 adults aged 50-80 years from the 2022 and 2024 Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys (KNHANES) and 2401 older adults aged 70-84 years from the 2016-2017 baseline of the Korean Frailty and Aging Cohort Study (KFACS). Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) and bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) were used to measure appendicular skeletal muscle mass (ASM). Age-group-specific contributors to sarcopenia were identified using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAPs) with temporal validation. Results In the KNHANES dataset, the mean age was 57.3 ± 4.4 years among middle-aged adults (50-64 years) and 72.6 ± 5.1 years among older adults ≥ 65 years. According to AWGS 2025 criteria, prevalence of possible sarcopenia, height-adjusted sarcopenia (ASM/height 2 + grip strength) and BMI-adjusted sarcopenia (ASM/BMI + grip strength) was 11.2%, 5.6% and 6.3% in middle-aged adults and 14.5%, 9.1% and 10.2% in older adults ≥ 65 years, respectively. Height-adjusted sarcopenia was more common in men among middle-aged adults but did not differ significantly by sex in older adults (p > 0.05). title: Sex-Specific Myostatin-Grey Matter Volume Associations in Ageing Adults: Implications for the Muscle-Brain Axis.
abstract: Background Sarcopenia is increasingly recognized as a risk factor for cognitive decline, suggesting bidirectional muscle-brain crosstalk mediated by myokines. Myostatin, a negative regulator of muscle growth, may influence brain health through systemic signalling, yet human neuroimaging evidence remains lacking. Moreover, men and women exhibit distinct patterns of muscle ageing and cognitive decline, but sex-specific effects of myostatin on brain structure have not been investigated. This study examined associations between serum myostatin and regional brain grey matter volume (GMV) in ageing adults, with emphasis on sexual dimorphism. Methods We analysed 482 community-dwelling participants (235 males, 247 females; mean age 67.2 ± 8.5 years, range of 50-88) from the I-Lan Longitudinal Aging Study. Serum myostatin levels, muscle mass and grip strength were assessed. High-resolution brain MRI was processed using voxel-based morphometry to examine associations between myostatin and regional GMV. title: Why Anthropologists Should Study Dogs.
abstract: While primates have traditionally been a focus of evolutionary anthropologists, the domestic dog represents a valuable complementary model due to its long shared evolutionary history with humans. The advantages of studying dogs are particularly evident in four key areas: (1) analyzing evolutionary adaptations, (2) understanding humanity's past, (3) examining humanity's cultural diversity, and (4) assessing factors that influence human health. Dogs have convergently evolved social cognition and local adaptations (including altitude adaptations and the ability to digest starches and lactose) that parallel those of humans, making them valuable models for testing evolutionary hypotheses. The global spread of dogs also illuminates human population histories, and isotopic analyses of dog remains can be proxies for human dietary data when sampling human remains is infeasible or inappropriate. Dogs' near-universal presence across human societies and exposure to the same real-world environments further make them uniquely powerful models for studying cultural variation and health.

title: Targeted modulation of protein post-translational modifications through induced proximity: advances and practical toolkits.
abstract: Targeted post-translational modification (PTM) of a protein of interest (POI) is achieved by inducing proximity to a protein-modifying effector enzyme in cells. A number of distinct induced proximity modalities, including genetically encodable polypeptides, small heterobifunctional molecules and molecular glues, can be applied to induce proximity between virtually any two intracellular proteins. Because targeted PTM can alter protein function and fate, induced proximity offers a route to target many proteins previously considered undruggable. With several molecular glue degraders long employed in clinic and one proteolysis-targeting chimera (PROTAC) recently FDA-approved for clinical use, induced proximity modality has emerged as clinically validated and rapidly expanding avenue for drug discovery. Beyond therapeutic applications, targeted PTM provides a versatile experimental platform for dissecting the functions and consequences of specific PTMs in physiological and disease contexts. In this review, we present an up-to-date overview of advances in targeted modulation of protein PTMs using induced-proximity technologies. We also highlight several induced-proximity toolkits and include practical information on them to facilitate their rapid adoption for proof-of-concept studies on targeted modulation of PTMs in cells.

title: Astragaloside IV and Ferroptosis Modulation in Pathological Cardiac Hypertrophy: Current Evidence, an Integrative Hypothesis, and Future Directions.
abstract: Pathological cardiac hypertrophy is initially an adaptive response to sustained mechanical, neurohormonal, or metabolic stress; however, it can progress to fibrosis, contractile dysfunction, arrhythmia, and heart failure. Ferroptosis is a type of regulated cell death caused by iron-dependent phospholipid peroxidation. Evidence consistent with ferroptosis, such as disrupted iron homeostasis, lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired antioxidant defense, has been reported in experimental models of pathological cardiac hypertrophy; however, these findings do not by themselves establish ferroptosis as a cause of hypertrophic remodeling. Astragaloside IV (AS-IV) is a cycloartane-type triterpene saponin from Astragalus species that has shown anti-hypertrophic, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, metabolic-regulatory and mitochondrial-protective effects in experimental cardiovascular models. AS-IV has also shown anti-ferroptotic effects in several cardiac and extra-cardiac disease models by means of Nrf2-centred antioxidant defense, regulation of SLC7A11/GPX4, p53 signaling, CD36-dependent lipid handling, and 14-3-3η-linked regulation of GPX4 stability. Nevertheless, whether ferroptosis inhibition directly contributes to the anti-hypertrophic effect of AS-IV in pathological cardiac hypertrophy remains unproven because direct causal validation in dedicated hypertrophy models is lacking. title: Impacts of Retrospective Lipid Suppression on Metabolite Quantification in Preclinical Proton MR Spectroscopic Imaging.
abstract: Extracranial lipid contamination remains a challenge in proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (MRSI), especially in short acquisition delay MRSI, where broad lipid resonances overlap with metabolite and macromolecular signals. Although retrospective lipid suppression techniques are widely used in human MRSI, their effects on metabolite quantification in preclinical MRSI, which is more prone to lipid contamination, have not yet been examined. In this study, we assessed how the retrospective lipid suppression and spectral fitting range influence spectral quality, spatial metabolite mapping, and quantification variability using proton MRSI of rat brains at 14.1 T. Lipid suppression was applied via an orthogonal projection method to both fully sampled and compressed sensing datasets, each comprising data with minimal and pronounced lipid contamination. Spectral fitting was performed with both broad (4.1-0.2 ppm) and narrow (4.1-1.8 ppm) ranges. When lipid contamination was minimal, suppression caused only slight spectral and spatial changes, with consistent metabolite quantification across conditions. In contrast, datasets with pronounced lipid contamination exhibited notable spectral changes following suppression, consequently affecting spatial metabolite mapping and concentration estimates. title: Separation of Anatomical Contributions in MRSI Using a Non-Negative Geographically Weighted Regression Model.
abstract: Magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (MRSI) is a non-invasive neuroimaging tool that maps brain metabolites, providing insights into brain physiology and pathology. However, clinical adoption remains limited due to low spatial resolution and partial volume effects, where acquired signals detect metabolism from different tissue types, preventing clear identification of tissue-specific metabolic patterns. We developed a statistical framework based on non-negative geographically weighted regression (NNGWR) designed to overcome these limitations. The method integrates tissue partial volumes with MRSI data using spatially adaptive regression to interpolate metabolite levels across the imaging volume while separating distinct tissue contributions. Importantly, our model accounts for spatial heterogeneity within tissues rather than assuming metabolic uniformity, providing more physiologically realistic estimates. Simulations using synthetic ground truth data show that our method consistently achieves a lower median absolute percentage error than cubic spline and zero-filling interpolations, especially under high noise or low-resolution conditions. A total of 120 MRSI datasets were acquired at 3 T from a cohort of 36 healthy volunteers to assess predictive performance. title: Associations between fruit, vegetable and fish and epigenetic markers of ageing and protein EpiScores in Generation Scotland
abstract: Consumption of foods such as fruit, vegetables and fish has been associated with a reduced risk of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) and greater longevity. These effects could, at least in part, be underpinned by epigenetic alterations, including changes in DNA methylation (DNAm) patterns. The aim of the current study was to characterise cross-sectional associations between three selected food components (fruit, vegetables and fish) and measures of DNA methylation associated with biological ageing (DNAm PhenoAge, DNAm GrimAge and DNAm Telomere Length), and epigenetic scores—or EpiScores—for 109 proteins in Generation Scotland. This study used dietary data collected on frequency and consumption quantities of fresh fruit ( n = 8648), vegetables ( n = 8686) and fish ( n = 5070). Linear regression models were used to test associations between food components and DNAm GrimAge, DNAm PhenoAge, DNAm Telomere Length, DNAm IL6 and the 109 EpiScores), After correction for multiple testing, there were several significant associations between food and the epigenetic biomarkers.. These findings provide additional evidence that dietary behaviours are associated with DNA methylation-derived biomarkers of ageing and health. Future research could focus on external validation of our results, and use longitudinal data to explore causal pathways.

title: Adropin ameliorates endometrial defects in letrozole induced hyperandrogenic mice.
abstract: Hyperandrogenism, a hallmark feature of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), is associated with endometrial dysfunction. Adropin, a hepatokine, has been reported to restore reproductive activity in PCOS mice. However, its role in uterine physiology remains elusive. Hence, the present study was undertaken to elucidate the effects of exogenous adropin treatment on endometrial functions in letrozole-induced hyperandrogenic (HA) mouse. Letrozole (6 mg/kg body weight) was given orally for 21 days to induce hyperandrogenism in female mouse. Thereafter, intraperitoneal injection of adropin (450 nmol/kg body weight) was given to HA mouse for 15 days. Decreased expression of adropin and its receptor GPR19 was observed in the uterus of HA mouse compared to vehicle control. title: Spermidine improves fast-twitch muscle histopathology and specific-force, and select bone properties, in the mdx mouse model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), an X-linked recessive disease, primarily affects skeletal and cardiac muscle, leading to progressive muscle wasting and weakness, but is also associated with compromised bone quality and microstructure. Human and mdx mouse studies show that DMD is associated with impaired muscle autophagy. The polyamine, spermidine, is known to stimulate autophagy, which some studies have linked to the upregulation of the microtubule-associated MAP1S protein. Spermidine has been shown to improve aspects of collagen VI deficiency-induced myopathy, in part, by reactivating autophagy. Thus, it was hypothesized that spermidine supplementation would improve the muscle pathology of DMD mdx mice, which would be associated with enhanced markers of autophagy and MAP1S. The impact of spermidine on bone quality or microstructure was also assessed using Synchrotron-generated x-ray imaging and 3-point bending. Three-week-old wild type (WT) and mdx mice were supplemented with 3 mM spermidine in drinking water for 13 weeks. Spermidine had no impact on mdx slow-twitch soleus muscle histopathology or contractile function, but improved mdx fast-twitch EDL muscle mass and specific tetanic force, which was associated with reduced centrally localized nuclei and tissue infiltrate. Surprisingly, despite a spermidine-induced increase in MAP1S protein, there was no change in markers of autophagy or autophagic flux. title: Host preference and larval performance of <i>Eueides isabella dianasa</i> (Hübner, 1806) (Lepidoptera: Nymphalidae: Heliconiinae) on <i>Passiflora</i> spp. (Malpighiales: Passifloraceae).
abstract: Passion fruit crops ( Passiflora spp.) are affected by several insect pests, including defoliating caterpillars such as Eueides isabella dianasa (Hübner, 1806) (Nymphalidae: Heliconiinae), a Neotropical butterfly distributed from the United States and Mexico to southern Brazil, whose larvae feed on multiple Passiflora species. Understanding plant-insect interactions through host preference and suitability is essential for supporting effective pest management. Therefore, the objectives of this study were (i) to evaluate host preference and leaf consumption of E. i. dianasa on different Passiflora species and (ii) to compare its developmental performance and survival on these hosts. Overall, Passiflora alata Curtis and Passiflora cincinnata Mast. showed lower host preference, whereas Passiflora edulis Sims was the most attractive host for E. i. dianasa at 3 and 10 days of larval age. Leaf consumption differed significantly among the Passiflora species, with P. edulis showing the highest consumption (95.15%), followed by P. cincinnata (24.54%) and P. alata (0.70%). Regarding developmental performance, host plant species did not affect the duration or weight of the larval and pupal stages. However, significant effects were observed on larval survival, larval and pupal viability, and adult longevity. title: From GLP-1 Receptor Agonism to Multi-Receptor Targeting in Kidney Disease.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists are established kidney-protective therapy in type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease, and co-agonists and multi-agonists that also target the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon receptors are advancing. Most reviews address these agents as a single class. This narrative review examines the three receptors separately, distinguishing the renal efficacy of a molecule from the causal contribution attributable to each of its receptor targets, and addresses three questions. First, what is known about the renal actions of each receptor: GLP-1 receptor agonism is the only receptor profile for which a drug (semaglutide) has shown kidney benefit in a dedicated outcome trial (FLOW), although the receptor-specific mechanism in humans is not established, as natriuresis is acute, not sustained, and hemodynamic effects are context-dependent; no GIP receptor-specific renal signature has been established in humans; and glucagon receptor signaling appears bidirectional, with potentially protective tubular actions coexisting with a risk of hyperfiltration. title: Effects of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 on Inflammation-Related Gene Expression in Adipose Tissue of Women with Obesity.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is known to have anti-inflammatory activity; however, its effects on the chronic low-grade inflammation present in the adipose tissue of individuals with obesity remain unclear. This study investigated the effect of GLP-1 infusion on inflammation related gene expression in the adipose tissue of women with obesity. Eleven women with obesity (BMI > 30 kg/m 2 ), aged 28-63 years, participated in a single blind, randomized, crossover study comparing 4 h infusions of synthetic human GLP-1 (7- 36) at 0.9 pmol/kg/min and saline after an overnight fasting. Total RNA was isolated from subcutaneous adipose tissue biopsies collected before and immediately after each infusion. Expression of 249 inflammation-related genes from the Human Inflammation Panel was assessed. Compared with saline infusion, an approximately two-fold increase in circulating GLP-1 induced by GLP-1 infusion significantly downregulated the expression of the pro-inflammatory genes TNF , C2 , CD4 , and MAPKAPK2 during the fasting state, with a near-significant reduction in MMP9 and IL8 expression. Upregulation of the anti-inflammatory regulator TOLLIP was also observed. Collectively, these results indicate an anti-inflammatory effect of GLP-1. Additionally, MAP2K1 , MAP2K4 , RIPK2 , and PLA2G4A , genes involved in adipose tissue remodeling, were upregulated during GLP-1 infusion. abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) is characterized by progressive cognitive decline and amyloid beta (Aβ) pathology, with emerging evidence indicating that autophagy-lysosomal dysfunction acts as an early pathogenic event. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying these processes remain incompletely understood. This study demonstrated that MCOLN1/TRPML1 (mucolipin TRP cation channel 1), a lysosomal Ca 2+ channel, was consistently downregulated in the hippocampus of patients with AD, five familial Alzheimer disease mutations (5xFAD) mice, and neuroblastoma Neuro-2a cells stably expressing human APP695 (N2a-APP) cells. Knockdown of Mcoln1 specifically in the hippocampus of mice recapitulated key AD-related phenotypes, including impaired lysosomal acidification, defective autophagic degradation, lysosomal enlargement, Aβ accumulation, dendritic spine loss, and cognitive deficits. Conversely, pharmacological activation with Mucolipin synthetic agonist 1 (ML-SA1) or genetic overexpression of MCOLN1 alleviated these abnormalities and mitigated Aβ pathology and cognitive impairments in 5xFAD mice. Mechanistically, decreased MCOLN1 protein impaired the vacuolar H + -ATPase (V-ATPase) assembly, potentially via diminished DMXL1 (Dmx like 1) phosphorylation through the Ca 2+ -CAMK2/CaMKII (calcium/calmodulin dependent protein kinase II) signaling pathway. title: Dietary selenium deficiency causes insulin-like growth factor 1 resistance in skeletal muscle of zebrafish.
abstract: Selenium (Se), an essential trace element for humans and animals, is critical for skeletal muscle homeostasis. Its deficiency is associated with low muscle mass due to the inhibition of the target of rapamycin complex 1 (TORC1)-mediated protein synthesis. However, the mechanism by which dietary Se deficiency hinders TORC1-mediated muscle protein synthesis remains unclear. Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1), a key upstream signaling molecule for TORC1, is pivotal in regulating muscle protein synthesis. This study evaluated whether dietary Se deficiency affects the transduction and transmission of IGF1 signaling in skeletal muscle using a zebrafish model, by manipulating dietary Se levels with Se-enriched yeast. Strikingly, dietary Se deficiency induced marked IGF1 resistance in skeletal muscle, characterized by elevated tissue IGF1 level but impaired transduction of both endogenous and exogenous IGF1 signaling from membrane receptor (IGF1 receptor/insulin receptor) to intracellular insulin receptor substrate 1 (IRS1). Mechanistically, dietary Se deficiency downregulated numerous antioxidant selenoproteins, increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, activated the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), and increased the phosphorylation of IRS1 at Ser 307 and Ser 312 sites, suggesting involvement of the ROS-mediated JNK-IRS1 pathway in dietary Se deficiency-induced IGF1 resistance. title: Dose optimization study of hydroxychloroquine as add-on therapy in patients with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus.
abstract: Objective Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is approved in India as third-line therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) at a recommended daily dose of 400 mg. However, concerns regarding cumulative retinal toxicity with long-term use highlight the need to identify the lowest effective dose. This study evaluated the efficacy and short-term safety of HCQ 200 mg, 300 mg, and 400 mg once daily in patients with inadequately controlled T2DM. Methods In this randomized, double-blind, multicentre dose-optimization trial, adults with inadequately controlled T2DM despite stable metformin and sulfonylurea therapy were randomized to receive HCQ 200 mg, 300 mg, or 400 mg once daily for 24 weeks. Efficacy endpoints included changes in glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c), fasting, postprandial glucose, and lipid parameters at Weeks 12 and 24. Safety was assessed through adverse-event, laboratory investigations, and ophthalmologic evaluations. Results Overall, 218 participants were randomized (mean age 48.22 ± 8.86 years; 58.7% male). At Week 24, mean HbA1c reductions from baseline were -0.64%, -0.78%, and -0.89% in the 200 mg, 300 mg, and 400 mg groups, respectively. Lipid parameters improved across groups. Sixteen participants experienced 23 adverse events; of which 82.6% unrelated to study medication. One serious adverse event, unrelated to HCQ, resolved without sequelae. title: Sarcopenia Assessment in Patients Post Metabolic Surgery With Suboptimal Weight Loss and Outcomes of Subsequent Liraglutide 3.0 mg.
abstract: Sarcopenia risk in post-metabolic surgery populations and in patients subsequently treated with Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) RA raises clinical concern due to potential long-term risks of muscle atrophy, frailty and disability. The aims of secondary data analysis from the BARI-OPTIMISE trial were to determine prevalence of baseline sarcopenia risk and examine the effects of 24 weeks of liraglutide 3.0 mg versus placebo in patients with suboptimal weight loss (WL) post primary metabolic/bariatric surgery (MBS) (sleeve gastrectomy and Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass) with a poor GLP-1 response. Forty-three patients (46.4 ± 9.8 years, BMI: 42.9 ± 7.37 kg/m2) ≥ 12 months post-MBS with suboptimal WL were given liraglutide 3.0 mg (n = 22), or placebo (n = 21) adjunct to lifestyle intervention (500-kcal daily deficit) for 24 weeks. DEXA measures for appendicular lean mass (ALM), arm lean mass (ARMLM) and body fat mass (BFM) and hand grip strength (HGS) were assessed at baseline and 24 weeks. Different sarcopenia risk methodologies/criteria were applied (EWGSOP2, FNIH and SDOC). Physical functioning tests (HGS, five-times sit-to-stand test [STS], STS power and 6 Minute Walk Test [6MWT]) were measured at baseline and 24 weeks. At baseline, using EWGSOP2 criteria for ALM, ALM index (ALMI) and HGS, 0%-36.4% of patients were at sarcopenia risk. title: Reduction in T-Cell Mitochondrial Respiratory Capacity After Reaching a Weight Loss Plateau.
abstract: Experiencing an involuntary weight loss plateau is common after behavioral weight loss. During such periods, sustained negative energy balance activates counterregulatory mechanisms that restore energy balance and may slow further weight loss. However, the cellular bioenergetic changes occurring specifically during a spontaneous weight loss plateau have not been investigated. We studied mitochondrial respiratory capacity in peripheral mononuclear cell populations from participants with obesity, both before and after an intensive lifestyle intervention (ILI). Body weight was tracked continuously over 18 months using a remote electronic scale, enabling retrospective categorization of outcome measures by weight loss phases: active weight loss (aWL), plateau (PL), or regain (RG). Differences in mitochondrial respiration were observed in T cells but not in monocytes across these phases. During aWL, mitochondrial respiratory capacity was similar to pre-ILI; however, basal, ATP-linked, maximal, and spare respiratory capacity were significantly lower during the PL and RG phases. In addition, ATP-linked respiration was lower in the PL and RG, despite higher mitochondrial citrate synthase activity in the PL relative to pre-ILI. These results indicate that T-cell bioenergetics may be responsive to shifts in energy balance during weight reduction. summary_short: These results indicate that T-cell bioenergetics may be responsive to shifts in energy balance during weight reduction.

title: β-Cell Function and Diabetes Outcomes 1 Year After Stopping Oral Baricitinib Immunotherapy for Type 1 Diabetes.
abstract: Objective The Baricitinib in New-Onset Type 1 Diabetes (BANDIT) trial showed that baricitinib treatment for 48 weeks preserved β-cell function and lowered insulin requirements and glucose in recent-onset type 1 diabetes. We aimed to determine the durability of these effects following treatment cessation. Research design and methods The following posttreatment outcomes of the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled BANDIT trial were analyzed: C-peptide and glucagon responses to a mixed meal, HbA1c, continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) measures, CD8+ T-cell phenotype and function, and adverse events. Results Of 91 randomized participants, 88 (58 baricitinib and 30 placebo) completed the week 96 follow-up. Mean ± SEM C-peptide was significantly greater in baricitinib-treated participants at week 72 (0.54 ± 0.05 vs. 0.38 ± 0.06 pmol/mL; P = 0.015) but not at week 96 (0.43 ± 0.05 vs. 0.35 ± 0.06 nmol/L; P = 0.336). No significant between-group differences in insulin dose, HbA1c, or CGM measures were observed during follow-up. Post hoc comparisons showed that when the study drug was ceased at week 48, baricitinib-treated adults (n = 28) experienced full preservation of β-cell function, whereas C-peptide decreased relative to baseline by 0.09 pmol/mL in baricitinib-treated children (n = 32; P = 0.022). We aimed to determine the durability of these effects following treatment cessation.

title: Gallbladder Gangrene Following Bevacizumab Therapy in Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia With Severe Hepatic Involvement and Functional Reclassification of a Synonymous ACVRL1 Variant.
abstract: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia type 2 (HHT2), caused by pathogenic variants in ACVRL1, frequently involves hepatic vascular malformations that may lead to high-output cardiac failure and ischemic biliary complications. Synonymous variants are often classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS) without transcript-level validation. We report an integrative clinical and molecular investigation of a patient with severe hepatic involvement and a synonymous ACVRL1 variant. Clinical, imaging, and longitudinal laboratory data were collected. Genetic testing was performed using whole-exome sequencing. Functional validation included a minigene splicing assay, RT-PCR analysis of patient-derived skin RNA, and quantitative PCR to assess ACVRL1 transcript expression. A heterozygous ACVRL1 c.474A>T synonymous variant was identified. Functional studies demonstrated activation of a cryptic splice donor site in exon 4, resulting in aberrant transcripts and approximately 50% reduction in ACVRL1 mRNA levels, consistent with nonsense-mediated decay. Clinically, the patient developed gallbladder gangrene following bevacizumab therapy in the setting of diffuse hepatic arteriovenous malformations. Subsequent sirolimus therapy was associated with stabilization of hemoglobin levels and hepatic parameters. summary_short: We report an integrative clinical and molecular investigation of a patient with severe hepatic involvement and a synonymous ACVRL1 variant. Subsequent sirolimus therapy was associated with stabilization of hemoglobin levels and hepatic parameters.

title: The Cardioprotective Effect of Fosinopril on Myocardial Infarction (MI) is Associated With the AMPK/mTOR Pathway.
abstract: To investigate the impact of fosinopril on cardiac function and its regulatory role in autophagy and the AMPK/mTOR pathway in a rat model of myocardial infarction (MI). MI was induced in rats by ligation of the left anterior descending coronary artery. MI modeling was verified by serum cardiac enzyme assays. Cardiac functions and histological change were determined by echocardiography, hematoxylin-eosin (HE) staining, and Masson's trichrome staining. Autophagy-associated factors were evaluated using western blotting and RT-qPCR. Apoptosis was analyzed by TUNEL assay, while alterations in the phosphorylation of the AMPK/mTOR pathway were determined by western blotting. Serum CK-MB and cTn-I levels were significantly elevated in MI rats, confirming myocardial injury. MI rats showed disordered myocardial architecture with inflammatory infiltration, compromised cardiac function (increased left ventricular end-systolic diameter and left ventricular end-diastolic diameter, decreased left ventricular fractional shortening and left ventricular ejection fraction) and myocardial fibrosis. Molecularly, RT-qPCR showed no significant changes in LC3 and p62/SQSTM1 mRNA levels, but Beclin-1 mRNA expression was elevated in MI rats and partially reversed by fosinopril. title: Insights Into Abdominal Wall Vascularized Composite Allotransplantation: An Individual Patient Data Analysis.
abstract: Background Abdominal wall vascularized composite allotransplantation (AWT) has emerged as a reconstructive option for patients with complex abdominal wall defects, particularly in conjunction with intestinal transplantation. Despite more than 2 decades of clinical experience, the available evidence remains limited to isolated case reports and small case series, and important questions regarding patient selection, operative techniques, immunosuppressive strategies, rejection patterns, and clinical outcomes remain unanswered. Therefore, we performed an individual patient data analysis to comprehensively evaluate the current evidence and provide insights into the clinical applicability, efficacy, and limitations of AWT. Methods We conducted a systematic review with an individual patient data analysis in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement. PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase were searched through December 2025. Results Twenty studies published between 2003 and 2023 reported 35 individual patients who underwent 37 AWT procedures. The median patient age was 37.5 years (IQR, 17.9), and follow-up ranged from 1 to 7 years. Alemtuzumab was used for induction in 32 patients (91.4%). The principal indications were large abdominal wall defects in 17 patients (48.6%), malignancy in 11 (31.4%), motility disorders in three (8.6%), and vascular disorders and congenital defects in two patients each (5.7%). title: Mitochondrial Dysfunction Across Renal Compartments in Diabetic Kidney Disease.
abstract: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) remains a leading cause of chronic kidney disease and kidney failure despite considerable therapeutic progress. Mitochondrial dysfunction has emerged as a central mechanism linking diabetic metabolic stress to progressive renal injury, yet it is often described as a generalized, whole-kidney abnormality. This view is incomplete because renal compartments differ in metabolic demand, substrate preference, oxygen exposure, mitochondrial density, and repair capacity. Therefore, diabetes is unlikely to induce a uniform mitochondrial defect across the kidney. Here, we introduce a compartment- and stage-specific framework that integrates evidence from proximal tubules, distal nephron segments, glomerular endothelial cells, podocytes, mesangial cells, immune cells, and interstitial compartments. Using this framework, we define how mitochondrial metabolism, dynamics, quality control, redox signaling, mtDNA stress, and inflammatory pathways contribute to DKD progression across distinct renal cell types. We highlight which mitochondrial programs are most clearly implicated in specific renal compartments, where evidence remains limited, and how understudied cell types may contribute to disease progression. This cell- and stage-specific framework provides a basis for interpreting mitochondrial dysfunction by renal compartment and biological context rather than as a single kidney-wide process. title: Schwann Cell-Specific ATG7-Dependent Autophagy Protects Myelin in a Mouse Model of Krabbe Disease.
abstract: Krabbe disease (KD) is a lysosomal storage disorder characterized by severe peripheral demyelination caused by mutations in galactosylceramidase (GALC), leading to the accumulation of galactosylceramide and psychosine. Although psychosine toxicity is central to KD pathology, additional mechanisms likely contribute to myelin dysfunction. Because Schwann cells (SCs) play a critical role in myelin maintenance, and GALC deficiency disrupts lysosomal function, we hypothesized that autophagy is altered in SCs during KD progression. Using a SC-specific Galc conditional knockout (Galc SC cKO) mouse model, we identified early changes in autophagy-related protein levels and increased autophagosome abundance during the pre-symptomatic phase, prior to detectable myelin abnormalities. To assess whether autophagy contributes to disease progression, we selectively deleted Atg7, an essential regulator of canonical autophagy, in SCs. Atg7 deletion alone did not affect myelin or behavior, but its loss in Galc SC cKO mice markedly worsened disease severity. Atg7-Galc SC cKO mice exhibited significantly thinner myelin and pronounced deficits in motor performance and nerve conduction, accompanied by altered steady-state levels of autophagy-associated proteins and functional decline. Notably, Atg7 deletion in Galc SC cKO mice did not further increase macrophage abundance, suggesting that the worsened myelin phenotype occurs without additional macrophage recruitment at this stage. title: Microgels Containing Protease-Resistant CXCL12 and FasL Enable Long-term Allo-Islet Function Without Systemic Immunosuppression.
abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a chronic disease characterized by the autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing β-cells in the pancreas. Replacement of β-cells by islet transplantation has proven to be successful in providing a functional cure for T1D. We previously showed that microencapsulation of allogeneic islets (allo-islets) or xenogeneic islets with CXCL12 promotes β-cell function, provides immune protection, and facilitates vascularization at the graft site in both small- and large-animal models of T1D. In addition, streptavidin-Fas ligand (SA-FasL) microgels induce immune acceptance of allo-islets through expansion of T regulatory cells (Tregs) in combination with short-term systemic immune suppression. This study evaluated a combination of these two complementary approaches for extending allo-islet graft survival in a mouse model of T1D through the codelivery of SA-CXCL12 or a protease-resistant variant of the chemokine (SA-prCXCL12) and SA-FasL within biotinylated microgels in an allogeneic-transplant setting. We demonstrated that microgels coated with SA-FasL and SA-prCXCL12, when cotransplanted with allo-islets, sustained long-term (6 months) diabetes reversal in streptozotocin-treated mice without any systemic immunosuppression more effectively than either agent alone. title: Support to Address Excess Weight and Related Physical Health Conditions for Young People With Severe Mental Illness: A Systematic Review With Narrative and Thematic Synthesis.
abstract: Background Young people with severe mental illness (SMI: psychosis, schizophrenia, and bipolar disorder) are at increased risk of experiencing excess weight and related health conditions, such as cardiovascular disease and Type 2 diabetes. Modifiable behavioural factors and antipsychotic-induced weight gain contribute to this risk. Earlier intervention to prevent and mitigate weight gain provides potential opportunity to improve long-term mental and physical health outcomes in this population. Aim To review support provided for young people with SMI, to address excess weight and related physical health conditions. Methods Three electronic databases were searched from January 2010 up to December 2025. Grey literature sources, and references and citations of included material were also searched. Full papers presenting qualitative or quantitative data on young people aged 12-18 years with SMI from high/very high development index countries were eligible for inclusion. Risk of bias for included studies was assessed using a validated tool for each study design. Data were synthesised through narrative and thematic synthesis. Results Seventeen articles describing 15 unique studies met inclusion criteria. title: Investigating the Effect of Gallic Acid During Acute and Chronic Exposure to Acetaldehyde in Liver Cells: Targeting Epigenetic Modifications.
abstract: Acetaldehyde (AcH), a toxic byproduct of ethanol metabolism, causes severe liver damage by binding to proteins and DNA and disrupting their functions. Despite extensive research, effective therapies for AcH-induced toxicity remain limited. This study investigated the protective role of gallic acid (GA), a natural polyphenol, against AcH-induced epigenetic and cellular alterations in WRL 68 cells following acute (24 h) and chronic (14 days) exposure. During acute exposure to AcH, the ability of GA to protect cells from AcH-induced cytotoxicity, DNA damage, and apoptosis was assessed using the MTT assay, DNA fragmentation, AO/EtBr dual staining assays, antioxidant analyses, and expression profiling of miRNAs and histone-modifying enzymes. GA (30 μM) significantly improved cell viability and reduced AcH-induced cytotoxicity, DNA damage, and apoptosis. It restored redox balance by enhancing SOD, catalase, and GSH levels and decreasing MDA levels. title: Blood-Derived DNA Methylation Biomarkers Predict Diabetic Kidney Disease and Map to Epigenomic Remodeling in Renal Cells.
abstract: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is a leading cause of end-stage kidney disease in type 1 diabetes (T1D); however, albuminuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) lack the precision necessary for early prognostication. We sought blood-derived DNA methylation biomarkers that predict DKD progression and reflect renal epigenomic remodeling. In the PROFIL cohort, we performed high-depth genome-wide methylation sequencing of leukocyte DNA from 101 adults with T1D and 20 control participants without diabetes, stratified by Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) risk and observed for a median of 5.6 years. Differentially methylated regions were identified across baseline KDIGO strata and prioritized based on hypomethylation, four or more CpGs per region, and discrimination between KDIGO categories; their associations with eGFR decline and rising albumin excretion were then evaluated. From these candidates, we derived a four-locus methylation risk score (MRS; SLC4A4, FSTL4, ICA1, and PTK2), validated by targeted assays in an independent subset of 330 participants with T1D with low or moderate KDIGO risk at baseline. Those with T1D showed global loss of 5-methylcytosine, with hypomethylated regions enriched at regulatory sites. title: Young ovarian tissue transplantation supports immune homeostasis in post-reproductive female mice through fertility-independent mechanisms
abstract: Reproductive aging is increasingly recognized as a driver of systemic decline in females, yet the ovarian mechanisms linking reproductive senescence to impaired health remain poorly defined. This study tested whether young ovarian tissue exposure supports peripheral immune homeostasis in post-reproductive female mice through fertility-independent mechanisms. Post-reproductive female CBA/J mice received young follicle-containing ovarian tissue transplants or remained as age-matched controls. Circulating immune mediators were analyzed using five multiplex cytokine panels comprising 200 analytes before and after treatment. Peripheral T-cell subsets and naive:memory ratios were assessed by flow cytometry, and thymic histopathology was evaluated at endpoint. Pre-treatment circulating immune profiles were indistinguishable between groups. At 577 days, transplant recipients showed higher AR, CD27L, EGF, IL-17E, IL-1ra, and B7-1/CD80 and lower P-selectin compared with controls. These changes were accompanied by an increase in peripheral memory CD4 + T cells (20.1 ± 4.2% vs. 15.0 ± 1.5%) and a nominal 64% higher CD4 + central naive:memory ratio, consistent with partial preservation of immune competence after reproductive senescence. title: Male chickadees with better spatial cognition sire more extra-pair young
abstract: Across animal taxa, females commonly mate with more than one male, even in monogamous mating systems. These extra-pair copulations and resulting young may increase the fitness of the female via a variety of mechanisms. The ‘good genes’ hypothesis suggests that socially monogamous females mate outside their pair bond to increase the fitness of their offspring via indirect genetic benefits, because extra-pair males do not provide parental care. We tested this hypothesis by quantifying extra-pair paternity in nonmigratory, food-caching mountain chickadees ( Poecile gambeli ). Chickadees rely on spatial cognition to recover scattered food caches, and variation in spatial cognition is associated with increased survival, longer lifespan, and is heritable. However, less is known about the role of sexual selection on spatial cognitive abilities. In the current study, we found that (1) males with better spatial cognitive abilities sired more extra-pair young and produced heavier offspring in their own nests compared to their poorer-performing counterparts, and (2) extra-pair males had significantly better spatial cognition than the social males they cuckolded. These results suggest that sexual selection shapes the evolution of spatial cognition in food-caching chickadees and are consistent with the good genes hypothesis, which posits that females gain indirect genetic benefits via extra-pair young.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists and pulmonary outcomes in rheumatoid arthritis: a propensity score-matched retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Pulmonary complications contribute substantially to morbidity and mortality in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), yet preventive strategies remain limited. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have metabolic and anti-inflammatory effects, but their association with respiratory outcomes in RA is unknown. Using electronic health record data from the TriNetX US Collaborative Network, we conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of adults with RA and type 2 diabetes mellitus who initiated GLP-1-based therapy or a DPP-4 inhibitor between January 1, 2016, and January 1, 2025. Primary coded outcomes were incident coded diagnoses of interstitial lung disease (ILD) and pulmonary hypertension (PH) over 3 years, with secondary outcomes including coded bronchiectasis, hospitalization, respiratory failure, mechanical ventilation, and all-cause mortality. Time-to-event analyses used Kaplan-Meier methods and Cox proportional hazards models. After matching, 1,656 patients were included in each cohort. Incident ILD occurred in 42 GLP-1RA users versus 54 DPP-4i users with no significant difference (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.57-1.29, p = 0.46). GLP-1RA use was associated with significantly reduced pulmonary hypertension (HR 0.47, 95% CI 0.33-0.68, p < 0.001), mechanical ventilation (HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.35-0.89, p = 0.013), respiratory failure (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.58-0.96, p = 0.023), and all-cause mortality (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.48-1.00, p = 0.047). title: A review of plant DNA ligases: evolution, molecular functions and applications in crop genetic improvement.
abstract: Genomic DNA constantly suffers endogenous and exogenous genotoxic damage throughout plant growth. DNA ligases catalyze nick sealing and serve core guardians of genome integrity. Plants harbor three major DNA ligase groups addressed in this review: the conserved LIG1 and LIG4 groups and the plant-specific LIG6 group. LIG1 is an essential housekeeping enzyme with dual nuclear-mitochondrial localization, participating in DNA replication, base excision repair and epigenetic demethylation. LIG4 dominates canonical non-homologous end joining for double-strand break repair and competitively balances homologous recombination. Unique LIG6 bears special structural domains and acts as a vital regulator of seed longevity and stress resistance. Despite functional descriptions, the spatiotemporal coordination mechanisms among these three ligases remain unclear. This review systematically summarizes the catalytic mechanisms, evolutionary divergence, subcellular distribution and multifunctional roles of plant DNA ligases, and discusses their application prospects in genome editing and crop seed improvement. Critical unresolved questions including LIG6 biochemical characterization and functional validation across diverse plant species are highlighted, and future research priorities are proposed to advance basic genome stability research and precision breeding utilization.

title: The Aging Surgeon: An American Society of Geriatric Otolaryngology Position Statement on Lifelong Competency and Career Transition.
abstract: BackgroundThe surgical workforce is aging, and projected workforce shortages may drive increasing demand for otolaryngologists to remain in practice later in their careers. Although aging brings heterogeneous cognitive, physical, and sensory changes, age alone is an inadequate predictor of professional competence. Existing guidance favors competency-based assessment over age-specific mandatory retirement, but no specialty-specific framework exists for otolaryngology-head and neck surgery (OHNS).ObjectiveTo review evidence on aging and surgical performance and develop recommendations to guide functional longevity and late-career transitions in OHNS.MethodsRecommendations were developed through a narrative review, refined iteratively, and approved by the American Society of Geriatric Otolaryngology (ASGO) Executive Council.ResultsChronological age alone is an inadequate predictor of surgical competence; studies of surgeon age and patient outcomes conflict. Available evidence favors individualized, longitudinal assessment of professional function rather than restriction based on age alone. ASGO identified principles emphasizing career-span assessment, transitions, institutional support, and physician dignity alongside patient safety. Important gaps remain, notably no validated specialty-specific assessment tools.ConclusionsAs more otolaryngologists practice later in their careers, specialty-specific, evidence-informed guidance is needed. title: Recurrent but not single falls are associated with frailty in community-dwelling adults aged 60 years and older in Chile.
abstract: Frailty encompasses multiple intrinsic fall risk factors, yet evidence from Latin America remains scarce. Most studies dichotomize frailty and falls, limiting understanding of how frailty phenotypes relate to single or recurrent falls. This study aims to determine the prevalence of single and recurrent falls and their association with frailty in Chilean community-dwelling adults. A cross-sectional analysis was conducted in 2,012 community-dwelling adults aged ≥ 60 years from the Alexandros cohort in Santiago, Chile. Falls in the past 12 months were self-reported (0, 1, or ≥ 2). Frailty was assessed considering the Fried phenotype adapted for Chile. Ordinal and binary logistic regression models estimated associations, adjusting for age, sex, BMI category, multimorbidity, and educational attainment. Robustness check and sex-stratified analyses were performed. Participants were 22.9% non-frail, 63.7% pre-frail, and 13.4% frail. Women had higher prevalence of frailty (16.0% vs. 8.3%) and recurrent falls (19.2% vs. 13.4%) than men. Recurrent falls were more frequent in frail participants than in non-frail and pre-frail peers (29.6% vs. 12.0% and 16.6%, p < 0.001). Frailty was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls (adjusted OR 2.00, 95% CI 1.45-2.77), whereas pre-frailty was not (OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.93-1.52). summary_short: Frailty was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls (adjusted OR 2.00, 95% CI 1.45-2.77), whereas pre-frailty was not (OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.93-1.52). Single falls were not significantly associated with frailty or pre-frailty.

title: A Japanese adolescent case of Chung-Jansen syndrome with obesity, diabetes mellitus and a rare missense variant of PHIP p.(Phe17Cys).
abstract: We report on a 13-year-old girl who presented with intellectual disabilities, behavioral abnormalities, dysmorphic features, obesity and diabetes mellitus. Whole-exome sequencing identified a rare PHIP variant (NM_017934.7: c.50T > G p.(Phe17Cys)) in the patient, corresponding to the diagnosis of Chung-Jansen syndrome. At age 16, oral aripiprazole treatment was initiated because behavioral problems and anxiety aggravated. Subsequently, chronic hyperglycemia and obesity worsened. At age 18, hemoglobin A1c and body mass index increased to 9.4% and 33 kg/m2. The initiation of subcutaneous insulin and tirzepatide therapy successfully improved her glycemic control. This is the first report to describe the detailed clinical phenotype of the PHIP p.(Phe17Cys) variant, providing valuable insight into pathogenicity despite its previous registration in ClinVar and gnomAD.
summary_short: At age 18, hemoglobin A1c and body mass index increased to 9.4% and 33 kg/m2. The initiation of subcutaneous insulin and tirzepatide therapy successfully improved her glycemic control.

title: Impact of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonist Treatment on Post-Operative Atrial Fibrillation.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists have demonstrated cardiovascular benefits with anti-inflammatory and anti-arrhythmic properties. This study aimed to evaluate the association of GLP-1 use with postoperative atrial fibrillation and mortality in patients undergoing cardiac surgery. This was a retrospective cohort study of patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery from 2010 to 2025. Patients were stratified into GLP-1 users and non-users. Patients with a history of atrial fibrillation (AF), concurrent MAZE procedure, and prior cardioversions or ablations were excluded. The primary outcome was incidence of new onset postoperative AF within 30 days. Secondary outcomes included AF-related readmissions and all-cause mortality. Multivariable adjusted regression models were used to compare POAF incidence and time-to-event secondary outcomes. A total of 8,672 patients were included. The 411 GLP-1 users were younger with higher BMI and HbA1c and were more likely to have diabetes compared to non-users (all p<0.001). After multivariable adjustment, GLP-1 users demonstrated a significantly lower incidence of postoperative AF compared to non-users (29.0% vs. 34.6%, RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.71-0.99, p=0.038). AF-related readmission in GLP-1 users were 1.2% at 1 year and 3.5% at 5 years, compared to 2.9% and 6.5% in non-users, respectively (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.30-1.13, p=0.111). title: Effect of CagriSema 2·4 mg/2·4 mg on glycaemic outcomes and their association with weight loss: a substudy of the randomised, double-masked, parallel-group, phase 3a REDEFINE 2 trial.
abstract: CagriSema 2·4 mg/2·4 mg, a fixed-dose combination of cagrilintide and semaglutide, demonstrated substantial weight loss versus placebo in adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes in REDEFINE 2. We aimed to evaluate glycaemic outcomes in a subgroup of participants who underwent continuous glucose monitoring (CGM). REDEFINE 2 was a global 68-week, double-masked, parallel-group phase 3a trial that included 1206 adults from 12 countries with a BMI of at least 27 kg/m2 and type 2 diabetes who were randomly assigned (3:1) to once-weekly subcutaneous CagriSema 2·4 mg/2·4 mg or placebo. Participants were assigned treatment using a centralised web-based system. Participants, investigators, site staff, and the sponsor were masked to group allocation throughout the trial. A subgroup of 199 participants from 35 US sites (including university hospitals, health-care centres, research centres, and other centres) were equipped with a CGM device (Dexcom G6 Pro) for double-masked measurements from week -3 to 0, week 20 to 24, and week 64 to 68. Prespecified secondary endpoints included change in time in range (TIR; 3·9-10·0 mmol/L) and change in time in tight range (TITR; 3·9-7·8 mmol/L) for CagriSema versus placebo. REDEFINE 2 is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05394519, and is completed. title: Impact of preoperative GLP-1 agonist use on patient-reported outcomes in obese patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty: a propensity score match analysis.
abstract: Obesity has traditionally been associated with increased perioperative risk in patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), originally developed for diabetes management, have recently emerged as an effective strategy for weight loss. Although recent literature has suggested that GLP-1 RA use may reduce postoperative complications following TKA, their impact on patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) remains unclear. A retrospective review of an institutional database identified 11,025 consecutive patients who underwent primary TKA. After exclusion, a 1:3 propensity score-matched analysis was performed to balance baseline demographic and clinical characteristics, yielding 146 obese patients who used preoperative GLP-1 receptor agonists and 438 matched non-users. Evaluated PROMs included SF-10a, PROMIS Global Mental and Physical, and KOOS-PS. Clinically meaningful improvement was assessed using the Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID). Secondary outcomes included 90-day and one- and two-year complications. There were no significant differences between GLP-1 RA users and non-users in preoperative or postoperative PROM scores, delta scores, or the proportion of patients achieving MCID improvement across SF-10a, PROMIS Global Mental, PROMIS Global Physical, or KOOS-PS (P > 0.05 for all). title: The Intrarenal See-Saw: Differentiating the Hemodynamic and Electrolyte Effects of Glucagon and Glucagon-Like-Peptide-1 Receptor Therapies.
abstract: The management of metabolic disease is undergoing a paradigm shift with the transition from single-agent glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) to novel dual GLP-1/glucagon receptor co-agonists. While GLP-1RAs offer established, weight-independent cardiorenal protection, the intentional therapeutic agonism of glucagon, a hormone historically targeted for suppression, introduces profound and largely unexamined physiological shifts. This review clarifies the distinct, often opposing, mechanisms of these hormones, focusing specifically on their divergent roles in kidney hemodynamics and tubular solute handling. Evolutionarily, glucagon defends against starvation by driving hepatic gluconeogenesis and ureagenesis, but its kidney hemodynamic effects are highly context-dependent. Experimental models suggest glucagon may trigger tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF)-mediated glomerular hyperfiltration via proximal Na+/amino acid co-transport after a protein meal, and via direct thick ascending limb (TAL) stimulation during fasting, though long-term human data remain limited. In contrast, GLP-1 coordinates the fed state, inducing proximal natriuresis via Na+/H+ exchanger 3 (NHE3) inhibition while concurrently acting as a kidney vasodilator, effectively uncoupling distal sodium delivery from tubuloglomerular feedback. title: Incretin-Based Medications for Obesity Management: Their Relationships to Mental Health, Eating Disorders, and Substance Use Disorders.
abstract: This narrative review examines the relationship between incretin-based medications (principally semaglutide and tirzepatide) and mental health, eating disorders, and substance use disorders. In obesity trials, semaglutide and tirzepatide did not worsen depressive symptoms or increase suicidal ideation or behavior, but most evidence comes from participants without major psychiatric illness. The medications consistently improved weight-related psychosocial quality of life, while effects on broader mental health quality of life were less consistent. Early data suggest potential benefit for binge eating disorder, though evidence remains limited. There are also concerns about misuse and possible worsening of restrictive eating in people with eating disorders. Preliminary findings indicate these drugs may reduce alcohol craving and heavy drinking, and there are limited data pertaining to other substance use disorders. Semaglutide and tirzepatide appear to have generally favorable mental health and psychosocial effects. However, more long-term, targeted studies of these and other novel incretin-based medications are needed in people with psychiatric illness, certain eating disorders, and substance use disorders.
summary_short: Early data suggest potential benefit for binge eating disorder, though evidence remains limited. Preliminary findings indicate these drugs may reduce alcohol craving and heavy drinking, and there are limited data pertaining to other substance use disorders.

abstract: In brief: GLP-1 receptor agonists can restore ovulation before reproductive safety is established, leaving many users in an unmanaged conception window. title: Comparative analysis of tyrosine kinase pathway inhibition, cell viability and immunohistochemical expression in canine and human urothelial carcinoma cell lines.
abstract: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder is a highly aggressive neoplasm in both humans and dogs, with the canine model representing a valuable tool for comparative oncology. This study aimed to characterize the immunohistochemical labelling of tyrosine kinases receptors (TKRs) and components of the MAPK pathway, as well as to evaluate the in-vitro response to targeted therapies in canine (AXC) and human (T24) urothelial carcinoma cell lines under two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) cell culture. Immunohistochemical analysis of the cell lines revealed greater labelling of VEGFR-2 and PDGFR-β, while EGFR and HER2 showed low or no immunolabelling, particularly in T24 cells. Functional assays demonstrated that lapatinib and sorafenib exerted the most pronounced cytotoxic effects in 2D culture, significantly reducing cell viability in both models. Toceranib also showed relevant activity, whereas rapamycin and palbociclib gave variable responses. Gene expression analysis, assessed by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction, showed that treatment with lapatinib and sorafenib modulated key genes, including EGFR, ERBB-2, c-KIT, MAPK, PDGFR-β and VEGFR-2. title: Effect of metformin on HIV reservoir, inflammation and cell differentiation in non-diabetic older people with HIV: a two-year placebo-controlled pilot trial (Metforaging).
abstract: People with HIV (PWH) on long-term antiretroviral therapy (ART) exhibit persistent inflammation, immune activation, and a stable HIV reservoir, contributing to non-AIDS age-related comorbidities. Metformin, an indirect mTOR inhibitor with immunometabolic properties, is a candidate geroprotective agent. We assessed its long-term immunological and virological impact in non-diabetic ART-suppressed PWH ≥50 years. Metforaging is a phase II, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial in which 35 non-diabetic ART-suppressed PWH ≥ 50 years received metformin or placebo for 96 weeks. At baseline and week 96, we quantified blood T-cell, monocyte, B-cell and NK subsets, inflammation and immune checkpoint biomarkers, total HIV DNA, intact/defective proviruses, and cell-associated HIV RNA (CA-RNA). Between-group effects were estimated by baseline-adjusted ANCOVA. At week 96, CD8+ TEMRA T cells increased with placebo but remained stable under metformin (adjusted mean difference -5.2%, 95% CI -8.5 to -2.0; p=0.003), with a modest increase in CD8+ effector memory T cells (p=0.044). No between-group differences were detected in soluble inflammation or immune checkpoint biomarkers, immune checkpoint mRNA expression, or HIV reservoir markers (total HIV DNA, intact and defective proviruses, CA-RNA). title: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is not associated with risk of incident inflammatory bowel disease in U.S. adults.
abstract: Some observational studies have linked higher dietary sugar intake to increased risk of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), though few studies have evaluated diabetes and IBD risk. Here, we examined the relationship between type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and incident IBD. We utilized data comprising 225 328 U.S. adults (mean baseline age 46 years) from the prospective Nurses' Health Study (1986-2020), Nurses' Health Study II (1991-2021), and Health Professionals Follow-Up Study (1986-2020). We excluded those with IBD at baseline and type 1 diabetes mellitus. We confirmed T2DM via validated questionnaires and IBD through medical record review. Using Cox proportional hazards models, we estimated hazard ratios and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC) according to diagnosis of T2DM, adjusting for confounders. We also examined hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) and metformin use and IBD risk. We documented 391 CD and 510 UC cases over 6 171 602 person-years of follow-up. T2DM was not associated with risk of CD (P = .28) or UC (P = .79). Compared with participants without T2DM, those with T2DM had an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.75 (95% CI, 0.44-1.27) for CD and 1.06 (95% CI, 0.69-1.62) for UC. In participants with available HbA1c (n = 5900), there was no association between having at least prediabetes (HbA1c ≥5.7) and risk IBD (all P ≥ .32). Metformin use was also not associated with IBD risk (all P ≥ .15). T2DM was not associated with incident CD o

title: Exercise to Enhance Mitophagy in Parkinson's Disease - A Narrative Review.
abstract: Mitophagy is a central mechanism in mitochondrial quality control and essential for neuronal health. It is impaired in Parkinson's disease (PD) and mutations of a number of genes associated with mitophagy cause familial PD. Recent advances in the development of novel treatment strategies for PD include phase I clinical trials for selective mitophagy enhancers. Next to pharmacological approaches, specific lifestyles, such as regular physical exercise, can promote mitophagy and thereby mitochondrial health and may be safer than pharmacological approaches and associated with many other health benefits. Here we explore, whether the well-known benefits of exercise for PD brain may be mediated by improved mitophagy. We put the potential benefits of mitophagy in the context of other exercise-induced, brain-health promoting mechanisms with relevance for PD and summarize the available literature investigating the role of mitophagy in therapeutic effects of exercise in models of PD. While the potential of exercise to promote mitophagy and brain health is well established, little direct evidence exists that implicates mitophagy as mediator of beneficial effects of exercise on PD symptoms and progression. Based on the identified knowledge gaps, we reflect on how this interaction may be studied in the future.
